title: Raven and the First Men
summary: Raven, the trickster-creator, finds the first humans hiding in a clamshell on the beach and coaxes them out into the world.
full_text:
In the time before time, the world was empty. There were no people, no villages, no fires. There was only the sea, the forest, and the sky. And there was Raven.

Raven was old — older than the trees, older than the mountains. He was the first being, and he was lonely. He flew over the water and saw nothing. He flew over the land and saw nothing. He perched on a driftlog and stared at the empty world.

Then he heard a sound. Not the wind, not the waves — something smaller. A clicking. A chirping. A sound like many small voices, coming from the beach.

Raven flew down. On the sand, half-buried in the tide, was a great clamshell. And inside the clamshell were people — tiny, curled up, packed tight like herring eggs. They were the first men, and they were hiding.

Raven leaned close. 'Come out,' he said.

The people did not move. They were afraid. The world outside the clamshell was vast and unknown. The sky was too big. The sea was too loud. The forest was too dark.

'Come out,' Raven said again. 'The world is waiting for you.'

A small voice piped up: 'What is the world?' 

Raven thought. 'The world is everything that is not the clamshell,' he said. 'It is the sun and the rain. It is the fish and the berries. It is the fire and the stories. It is the women and the children. It is the dancing and the singing. It is the living and the dying. It is everything.'

The people were silent. Then the small voice said: 'Is it safe?' 

Raven laughed. 'No,' he said. 'The world is not safe. But it is beautiful. And it is yours, if you want it.'

One person stood up. He was small, with curious eyes and trembling hands. He climbed to the rim of the clamshell and looked out. The sun was rising over the water, turning the sea to gold. The trees were green and tall. The birds were singing.

'It is beautiful,' he said.

He stepped out. The sand was warm under his feet. The air smelled of salt and cedar. He took another step, and another, and the world opened around him like a flower.

The others followed. One by one, they climbed from the clamshell and stepped into the world. Some ran to the water. Some ran to the trees. Some stood still, staring at the sky.

Raven watched. He was pleased. The world was no longer empty.

But the people had no fire. They had no stories. They had no songs. They had only the clamshell and the sand.

Raven flew to the sky and stole the sun. He brought it down and placed it in the people's hands. 'This is fire,' he said. 'Keep it burning.'

He flew to the mountain and stole the salmon. He brought them to the people. 'This is food,' he said. 'Share it.'

He flew to the ancestors and stole the songs. He brought them to the people. 'This is culture,' he said. 'Remember it.'

The people built their villages. They caught their salmon. They sang their songs. They told their stories. And every year, when the first salmon run came, they left a gift on the beach — a piece of cedar bark, placed inside a clamshell — to remember where they came from.

Raven flies overhead. He still watches. He still tricks. He still steals. But he is no longer lonely.

Because the world is full of people, and the people are full of stories, and the stories are full of Raven.
moral: The world is not safe, but it is beautiful. That is enough reason to step out of the clamshell.
source: Based on Haida oral traditions from Haida Gwaii, British Columbia.
